notes.text: In a 12-month randomized trial comparing alternate-day fasting (ADF) with daily calorie restriction (CR), weight loss was 6.0% with ADF versus 5.3% with CR; the difference was not significant. The trial concluded ADF did not produce superior adherence, weight loss, weight maintenance, or cardiovascular-risk improvements. Dropout was 38% with ADF versus 29% with CR.

A separate zero-calorie ADF pilot reported no between-group difference in weight regain over weeks 8–32; reported body-composition changes during regain were CR: +1.2 ± 0.8 kg fat mass (FM) and +1.1 ± 0.5 kg lean mass (LM), versus ADF: −0.4 ± 0.8 kg FM (p=0.173 vs CR) and +2.0 ± 0.5 kg LM (p=0.197 vs CR). The snippet does not establish that this pilot had at least 12 months’ follow-up.

In the 12-month randomized trial by Liu et al., 139 adults with obesity were assigned to time-restricted eating (TRE) plus calorie restriction (n=69; eating 8:00 a.m.–4:00 p.m.) or daily CR alone (n=70). Both groups were instructed to consume 1,500–1,800 kcal/day for men and 1,200–1,500 kcal/day for women.

At 12 months in the Liu trial, mean weight change was −8.0 kg (95% CI −9.6 to −6.4) with TRE plus CR and −6.3 kg (95% CI −7.8 to −4.7) with daily CR; the net difference was −1.8 kg (95% CI −4.0 to 0.4; P=0.11), not statistically significant.

In the Liu trial, 135/139 participants (97.1%) completed the 6-month intervention and 118/139 (84.9%) completed the 12-month follow-up. Adherence was defined as the mean percentage of days participants adhered to both prescribed calories and the eating period, but the available excerpt gives no adherence values.

A 12-month randomized comparison of intermittent (5:2) versus continuous energy restriction in healthy overweight or obese adults is cited as Headland et al., International Journal of Obesity (2019), 43:2028–2036, DOI 10.1038/s41366-018-0247-2. The available excerpts do not provide its numerical weight outcomes, adherence, dropout, regain, or achieved-intake comparison.

A 2022 meta-analysis excerpt reports that across intermittent-energy-restriction comparisons, study energy intakes were comparable between groups in 17 trials, lower in the intermittent-restriction group in 5, and unreported in 6; its included trials ranged from 2–52 weeks, so this is not itself evidence for a ≥12-month head-to-head trial.

Thomas et al. (2022) compared early TRE plus CR with daily CR for 39 weeks (12-week intervention plus 27-week follow-up), shorter than the requested 12-month threshold; reported weight loss at 39 weeks was 5.2% versus 4.7%, respectively.

Network estimates combine direct and indirect evidence and should not be conflated with direct randomized comparisons at 12 months.
Review-level pooled findings do not establish whether a small weight difference is clinically meaningful or whether calorie intake/adherence explains it.
Population representation, including underrepresented adult groups, was not extractable from the retrieved material beyond the review's broad description.

decisions: b8: supported. s14, s20 and s22 give −8.0 kg versus −6.3 kg and 118/139 (84.9%) completing 12 months. The −1.8 kg (95% CI −4.0 to 0.4; P=0.11) comes from the Long-Term Trials Researcher's full-text excerpt, and s20 says no significant difference. Superiority was correctly not claimed.

b11: weak. 118/139 (84.9%) is supported by s14. The 135/139 six-month completion figure is not in the s20 snippet.
b2: weak. The −1.69 kg and −1.05 kg estimates and the 'moderate-certainty' label are not visible in the s1 or s3 excerpts that were cited.

observations: Only Liu et al. (about 12 months, with equal calorie targets) and Trepanowski et al. (12 months) give direct ≥12-month evidence. Both show no significant difference between intermittent fasting and daily restriction.
The Liu 12-month data have a CI that spans zero (−4.0 to 0.4), so the trial neither shows equivalence nor rules out a modest TRE benefit.

The BMJ ADF −1.29 kg estimate comes from a network meta-analysis that includes indirect comparisons and mostly shorter trials, so it should not be read as a durable 12-month benefit. The Evidence Synthesis Researcher raised the same point.
Attrition differed in Trepanowski et al. (38% versus 29%). That favours neither arm on adherence.
critiques: Several cited sources are search snippets, not full text. Numeric claims in b2, b5, b10, b11 and b13 cannot be checked against what was shown.
b9 cites popular-press sources (s15 NutritionFacts, s16 ScienceDaily) instead of the primary JAMA Intern Med paper. The primary paper (s24) was found only through my own search.

The brief never states that the Liu 12-month result is a week-12-month follow-up of a 6-month intervention. Whether participants kept restricting in the second 6 months is unclear and bears on the 'sustained' question.
The Headland 5:2 trial (b12) has no numeric results, so the ≥12-month evidence base is just two trials, both with CIs spanning zero for between-group differences.

data.summary: Editor is writing Executive summary
Editor wrote Executive summary

blocks.text: The verified direct 12-month comparisons do not demonstrate greater weight loss with intermittent fasting than with daily calorie restriction. Time-restricted eating plus calorie restriction and alternate-day fasting both produced weight loss, but neither significantly outperformed daily restriction. This is not proof of equivalence: uncertainty remains about meaningful differences, other fasting protocols, and maintenance beyond one year. Overall confidence is moderate.
blocks.author: editor

data.summary: Editor is writing Key findings

blocks.text: The BMJ review reported a small body-weight advantage for alternate-day fasting over continuous energy restriction, with mean difference −1.29 kg; this pooled finding alone does not establish a 12-month sustained effect.
blocks.author: researcher-2

comments.text: s3: ADF was 'the only intermittent fasting diet strategy to show a small benefit' vs continuous energy restriction (mean difference −1.29 kg). The brief correctly says this does not establish a 12-month sustained effect. s3's headline says intermittent fasting is 'comparable' to traditional diets.
comments.author: verifier

blocks.text: In the 12-month randomized Liu et al. trial of 139 adults with obesity, TRE plus calorie restriction resulted in mean weight change of −8.0 kg versus −6.3 kg with daily calorie restriction; the between-group difference was −1.8 kg (95% CI −4.0 to 0.4; P=0.11), so superiority was not established.
blocks.author: researcher-1

comments.text: s14: 118/139 (84.9%) completed 12 months; −8.0 kg (95% CI −9.6 to −6.4) with time-restricted eating. s20: −6.3 kg (−7.8 to −4.7) with daily calorie restriction, 'no significant difference'. The net −1.8 kg (95% CI −4.0 to 0.4; P=0.11) comes from the teammate's full-text excerpt. The 'superiority not established' framing is correct.
comments.author: verifier

blocks.text: A 12-month ADF-versus-daily-restriction randomized trial reported weight loss of 6.0% with ADF versus 5.3% with daily restriction, with no statistically significant difference; dropout was 38% versus 29%, respectively.
blocks.author: researcher-1

comments.text: s16 supports 6.0% vs 5.3% at one year with no significant difference. The 38% vs 29% dropout is not in s15 or s16. It is confirmed only by s24 (13/34 [38%] ADF vs 10/35 [29%] daily calorie restriction), which is not cited, so the citation is incomplete.
comments.author: verifier

blocks.text: No numerical Headland 5:2-versus-daily-restriction weight loss, maintenance/regain, or attrition estimate was verified in this round; therefore no comparative effect or equivalence conclusion can be drawn from the retrieved evidence.
blocks.author: researcher-1

comments.text: s32 is only a PubMed title/identification record ('Effect of intermittent compared to continuous energy restriction on weight loss and weight maintenance after 12 months in healthy overweight or obese adults'). It has no numbers, so the claim is accurate. The 24-month s34 statement is secondary and is not a substitute.
comments.author: verifier

blocks.text: The available Trepanowski trial summary states that ADF did not produce superior adherence or weight maintenance compared with daily calorie restriction.
blocks.author: researcher-2

comments.text: The s25 PubMed abstract says 'Alternate-day fasting did not produce superior adherence, weight loss, weight maintenance, or cardioprotection vs daily calorie restriction.' The visible s16 snippet covers only weight loss, so s25 should be cited.
comments.author: verifier

blocks.text: The Trepanowski ADF-versus-daily-restriction trial was a single-center study of 100 adults recruited in Chicago; participants had obesity (mean BMI 34), mean age 44 years (SD 11), and were 86 women and 14 men, limiting generalization to men, other settings, and populations without obesity.
blocks.author: researcher-3

comments.text: s40 confirms 100 participants, 86 women and 14 men, and mean age 44 years. The snippet does not show single-center status, Chicago, mean BMI 34, or the age SD. The generalization limit is plausible but only partly verified.
comments.author: verifier

blocks.text: In Liu et al.’s 12-month randomized trial, time-restricted eating plus calorie restriction produced −8.0 kg weight change versus −6.3 kg with daily restriction. The between-group difference was −1.8 kg (95% CI −4.0 to 0.4; P=0.11), so superiority was not established.
blocks.author: editor

blocks.text: In Trepanowski et al.’s 12-month trial, weight loss was 6.0% with alternate-day fasting versus 5.3% with daily restriction, without a statistically significant difference. The primary abstract also reports no superior adherence or weight maintenance.
blocks.author: editor

blocks.text: The BMJ review reported a small pooled alternate-day fasting advantage over continuous restriction (−1.29 kg). The supplied evidence does not establish that this advantage persists in direct comparisons at 12 months or longer.
blocks.author: editor

blocks.text: A 2025 BMJ systematic review and network meta-analysis included 99 randomized clinical trials involving 6,582 adults with varied health conditions.

comments.author: verifier

blocks.text: A separate systematic review of 28 trials (7 TRE, 10 ADF, 11 5:2) included interventions lasting 2–52 weeks, so it does not provide evidence of sustained 12-month comparative effects.
blocks.author: researcher-2

comments.text: The s8 title confirms a meta-analysis of intermittent versus continuous energy restriction in adults. The 28 trials, the 7/10/11 split and the 2-52 week range are not visible, and the no-12-month conclusion depends on that range.

data.summary: Editor wrote Evidence

blocks.text: Liu et al. randomized 139 adults with obesity; 118 (84.9%) completed the 12-month follow-up. This trial tests adding an eating-time restriction to calorie restriction, rather than fasting without calorie restriction.
blocks.author: editor

blocks.text: The alternate-day fasting trial included 100 participants across three groups, including a control group. Dropout was 13/34 (38%) with alternate-day fasting versus 10/35 (29%) with daily restriction.
blocks.author: editor

blocks.text: Headland et al.’s intermittent-versus-continuous restriction study is identified as a 12-month weight-loss and maintenance comparison in healthy adults with overweight or obesity. Its numerical outcomes were not verified, so it cannot support a comparative effect estimate here.
blocks.author: editor

data.summary: Editor is writing Arguments

blocks.text: In the BMJ review's studies of at least 24 weeks, continuous energy restriction was associated with 2.21 kg greater weight loss than an ad-libitum diet; this comparison is not fasting versus calorie restriction.
blocks.author: researcher-2

comments.text: The s7 snippet does not show the 2.21 kg figure or the ≥24-week condition. The draft already says this is not a fasting-vs-calorie-restriction comparison, which is correct.
comments.author: verifier

blocks.text: A 2022 meta-analysis excerpt reported comparable study energy intakes between groups in 17 trials, lower intermittent-restriction intake in 5, and unreported intake in 6; its included studies lasted 2–52 weeks, so it cannot answer the ≥12-month direct-comparison question.
blocks.author: researcher-1

comments.text: The 28 trials and 2–52 week range are consistent with s8, and the draft correctly says it cannot answer the ≥12-month question. The 17/5/6 intake split is not in the visible snippet.
comments.author: verifier

blocks.text: The ADF trial enrolled metabolically healthy obese adults and was conducted at one academic institution, so it does not directly establish comparative effectiveness for adults with metabolic disease or broader clinical populations.
blocks.author: researcher-3

comments.text: The trial title ('metabolically healthy obese adults', cited in s26) supports the population claim. 'One academic institution' is not in the supplied text. The inference that results do not extend to metabolic disease is reasonable but is the brief's own inference.
comments.author: verifier

data.summary: Editor wrote Arguments

blocks.text: Direct 12-month randomized comparisons deserve greater weight for this question than pooled estimates combining durations and direct or indirect comparisons. The two comparisons with verified numerical outcomes agree that fasting superiority was not demonstrated.
blocks.author: editor

blocks.text: An eating schedule may be a useful way to implement weight management without being intrinsically more effective. The available evidence supports offering fasting as an alternative, not promising additional sustained loss from fasting itself.
blocks.author: editor

data.summary: Editor is writing Counterarguments
Editor wrote Counterarguments

blocks.text: Failure to reach statistical significance does not establish equivalence. Liu’s confidence interval remains compatible with up to 4.0 kg greater loss from adding time restriction; the alternate-day fasting comparison is small, and its between-group confidence interval was not verified. This limits certainty about the size of any advantage, but does not justify claiming superiority.
blocks.author: editor

blocks.text: The pooled −1.29 kg alternate-day fasting advantage is evidence against dismissing all potential benefits. However, without a verified ≥12-month subgroup, it does not change the conclusion about sustained superiority.
blocks.author: editor

blocks.text: The evidence assembled here is incomplete across fasting protocols. Unverified Headland outcomes and an identified 2025 4:3 fasting study summary leave open whether another regimen performs better; neither supplies usable comparative estimates in this material.
blocks.author: editor

data.summary: Editor is writing Risks
Editor wrote Risks

blocks.text: Attrition may affect long-term estimates and practical acceptability. Higher observed dropout with alternate-day fasting should not be interpreted as a proven tolerability difference without further analysis.
blocks.author: editor

blocks.text: Generalization is limited: the alternate-day fasting trial included 86 women and 14 men and concerned metabolically healthy adults with obesity. These results do not establish comparative effectiveness for every adult population.
blocks.author: editor

blocks.text: A weight difference at 12 months does not by itself establish durable maintenance after treatment ends. Verified post-intervention regain and achieved-intake data are insufficient.
blocks.author: editor

data.summary: Editor wrote Open questions

blocks.text: What are the numerical between-group outcomes, uncertainty, attrition, and maintenance results in Headland’s 12-month trial and the identified 4:3 fasting comparison?
blocks.author: editor

blocks.text: Across direct ≥12-month trials, how do achieved calorie intake, adherence, and weight regain differ by fasting protocol?
blocks.author: editor

blocks.text: Do advantages emerge beyond one year or in specific populations, and can adequately powered comparisons exclude clinically meaningful differences?
blocks.author: editor

data.summary: Editor wrote Recommendation

blocks.text: Neither approach wins on demonstrated sustained weight loss in the verified 12-month comparisons. Favor daily calorie restriction when a regular daily eating pattern is easier to maintain; consider intermittent fasting when the person prefers that schedule, without promising greater loss. Confidence is moderate that superiority has not been demonstrated, but lower that the approaches are truly equivalent. The conclusion would change with verified, sufficiently precise direct ≥12-month evidence showing a meaningful fasting advantage and acceptable retention.
